Maladaptive Strategies.value: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings
avoid anything that could be stressful
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something about me that made the event happen
My life has been destroyed by the trauma
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

issues.item: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: 'Never Alone' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of police violence and the rest of the profile. This item more strongly suggests fear of being alone with a potentially abusive intimate or familiar person, whereas the threat items center on strangers and general vigilance. That mismatch is difficult to explain clinically within the same trauma-linked profile.

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Contamination' is not well aligned with the trauma type and accompanying appraisals. Feeling dirty or contaminated is more characteristic of sexual trauma; with police violence, and with the current memory/threat content, this appraisal stands out as clinically incongruent rather than merely unusual.

vignette:
Arthur, a respected 58-year-old dentist, presented with a profound sense of unease that had permeated every aspect of his life since an incident of police violence two years prior. He had been walking home late from his practice when he was caught in a chaotic street protest. Despite identifying himself as a medical professional, he was violently pushed to the ground, a knee pressed hard into his back, and held there while officers shouted over him. The sharp, searing pain in his lower back, the metallic tang of fear, and the deafening shouts of "Get back! Don't move!" echoed in his mind long after the physical ordeal ended.

Now, those sounds often return unbidden. When memories of what happened surface, Arthur sometimes hears those very shouts in his head, a vivid auditory recall that instantly transports him back to the pavement. To prevent these disorienting intrusions from taking hold, he began to actively numb himself, avoiding anything that could stir strong feelings, positive or negative. These intrusive sensory memories immediately put Arthur on high alert, causing him to feel a pervasive threat from strangers approaching him, even in ordinary situations like a new patient entering his operatory. This constant feeling of threat, particularly when patients lean over him or approach his dental chair, has led Arthur to compulsively scan his surroundings. He finds himself checking for exits or potential threats in his own office, a habit that began subtly but has become second nature.

This hypervigilance and perceived threat have also profoundly influenced Arthur's behaviour, leading him to avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, a desperate attempt to numb himself to the overwhelming anxiety. He also makes a concerted effort to avoid stressors, delegating complex procedures and shortening his work hours, which has started to impact his practice. His efforts to avoid all feelings and avoid stressors have inadvertently made the memory of the event more fragmented and alien. The less he engaged with his own emotions, the more disconnected he felt from his own past, paradoxically making the memory feel like it belongs to someone else rather than to him, rather than integrating into his life story.

Each time the pain recall or auditory recall surfaced, it reinforced Arthur's conviction that his life had been destroyed by the trauma. The sheer unfairness of the event, replayed in his mind through these vivid sensory intrusions, solidified his belief that what happened to him was deeply unfair and nothing had been done about it. This profound sense of injustice, coupled with a nagging thought that there was something about him that made the event happen, made it impossible for him to process the memory. These negative appraisals kept the memory stuck, ensuring it continued to feel alien and raw, rather than allowing it to fade or integrate.

As Arthur increasingly tried to avoid stressors and avoid all feelings, he felt more isolated and less capable of living his life, which only deepened his appraisal that his life had been destroyed. He saw his avoidance as proof that he was fundamentally broken. The persistent trouble falling or staying asleep, coupled with the constant vigilance, the feeling of threat from strangers, eroded Arthur's sense of safety and normalcy. This perpetual state of alert solidified his belief that his life had been destroyed by the trauma, as he could no longer function as he once did. His constant checking surroundings and vigilance for threat would often inadvertently trigger fragmented auditory recall or pain recall, as his hyper-alert nervous system was primed to interpret any sensory input as a potential re-enactment of the trauma. He also found himself always choosing where to sit based on how safe or protected he felt, whether it was in his dental office during a lunch break or in a restaurant with his partner, always needing his back to a wall.

Arthur's partner eventually insisted he seek help, noticing his increasing withdrawal and the way he flinched at sudden noises. He came to therapy exhausted, his dental practice suffering, and deeply afraid that he would never feel safe or whole again, stuck forever in a loop of fear and avoidance.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not explicitly convey that the trauma memory directly influences or leads to maladaptive strategies; instead, this relationship is mediated by a sense of threat.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
